'''boulon''' (bö′lon), ''n.'' [Native name.] A harp with fibrous strings, used by the negroes of Senegambia and Guinea.

'''boultel<sup>1</sup>†''', ''n.'' Same as ''boltel.''

'''boun†''' (boun), ''v.'' [< ME. ''bounen'', ''bownen'', < ''boun'', prepared: see ''boun'', ''a.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To prepare; make ready.
{{smaller block|The kyng boskes lettres anon, to ''bownen'' his bernes [men].

{{smaller block|<poem>So mourned he, till Lord Dacre’s band

{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., v. 30.}}</poem>}}

{{right|''Scott'', Harold the Dauntless, iv. 14.}}</poem>

'''boun†''' (boun), ''v.''   [< ME. ''bounen'', ''bownen'', < ''boun'', prepared: see ''boun'', ''a.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' To prepare; make ready.
{{smaller block|The kyng boskes lettres anon, to ''bownen'' his bernes [men].
{{right|''Joseph of Arimathie'' (ed. Skeat), l. 414.}}}}
{{smaller block|I wold ''boun'' me to batell. {{right|''Destruction of Troy'', l. 827.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To make ready to go; go: as, to busk and ''boun'', a common expression in old ballads.
{{smaller block|<poem>So mourned he, till Lord Dacre’s band
Were ''bowning'' back to Cumberland.
{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., v. 30.}}</poem>}}

'''bounce''' (bouns), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''bounced'', ppr. ''bouncing''.   [Early mod. E. also ''bounse'', < ME. ''bounsen'', ''bunsen'', beat, strike suddenly; cf. LG. ''bunsen'', G. dial. ''bumbsen'', beat, knock, = D. ''bonzen'', bounce, throw; cf. D. ''bons'', a bounce, Sw. ''bus'', dial. ''bums'' = G. ''bums'', ''bumbs'', ''bumps'', adv. interj., at a bounce, at once; cf. Icel. ''bops'', imitating the sound of a fall. All prob. orig. imitative; cf. ''bound''<sup>2</sup> and ''bump''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To beat; thump; knock; bang.
{{smaller block|<poem>Wilfully him throwing on the gras
Did beat and ''bounse'' his head and brest ful sore.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. xi. 27.}}</poem>
He ''bounced'' his head at every post. {{right|''Swift.''}}}}

'''2.''' To cause to bound or spring: as, to ''bounce'' a ball.—'''3.''' To eject or turn out without ceremony; expel vigorously; hence, to dismiss or

41 discharge summarily, as from one’s employment or post. [Slang, U. S.]

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To beat hard or thump, so as to make a sudden noise.
{{smaller block|<poem>Yet still he bet and ''bounst'' upon the dore.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., V. ii. 21.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Up, then, I say, both young and old, both man and maid a-maying,
With drums, and guns that ''bounce'' aloud, and merry tabor playing!</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Burning Pestle, iv. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|Another ''bounces'' as hard as he can knock. {{right|''Swift.''}}}}
'''2.''' To spring or leap against anything, so as to rebound; beat or thump by a spring; spring up with a rebound.
{{smaller block|<poem>Against his bosom ''bounc’d'' his heaving heart.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Pal. and Arc., i. 556.}}}}
'''3.''' To leap or spring; come or go unceremoniously.
{{smaller block|As I sat quietly meditating at my table, I heard something ''bounce'' in at the closet-window.
{{right|''Swift'', Gulliver’s Travels, ii. 5.}}}}
'''4.''' To boast or bluster; exaggerate; lie.
{{smaller block|He gives away countries, and disposes of kingdoms; and ''bounces'', blusters, and swaggers, as if he were really sovereign lord and sole master of the universe.
{{right|''Bp. Lowth'', Letter to Warburton, p. 14.}}}}
{{smaller block|If it had come to an oath, I don’t think he would have ''bounced'', neither; but, in common occurrences, there is no repeating after him. {{right|''Foote'', The Liar, ii. 1.}}}}

'''bounce''' (bouns), ''n.''   [< ''bounce'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' A sudden spring or leap.—'''2.''' A bound or rebound: as, you must strike the ball on the ''bounce''.—'''3.''' A heavy blow, thrust, or thump.

{{smaller block|I heard two or three irregular ''bounces'' at my landlady’s door, and upon the opening of it, a loud cheerful voice inquiring whether the philosopher was at home.
{{right|''Addison'', Sir Roger at Vauxhall.}}}}
'''4†.''' A loud heavy sound, as of an explosion; a sudden crack or noise.
{{smaller block|I don’t value her resentment the ''bounce'' of a cracker.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', She Stoops to Conquer, iii.}}}}
'''5.''' A boast; a piece of brag or bluster; boastful language; exaggeration.—'''6.''' A bold or impudent lie; a downright falsehood; a bouncer. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|<poem>“Why, whose should it be?” cried I, with a flounce;
“I get these things often;”—but that was a ''bounce''.</poem>
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Haunch of Venison, l. 42.}}}}
{{smaller block|Oh, Cicero! . . . not once did you give utterance to such a ''bounce'' as when you asserted, that never yet did human reason say one thing, and Nature say another.
{{right|''De Quincey'', Secret Societies, i.}}}}
'''7.''' Expulsion; discharge; dismissal. [Slang, U. S.]—'''8.''' [Perhaps of diff. origin.] A local English name of the dogfish or shark, ''Scylliorhinus catulus''.—'''To get the grand bounce,''' {{smaller|to be put out or discharged summarily from one’s post or employment. [Slang, U. S.]}}

'''bounce''' (bouns), ''adv.''   [< ''bounce'', ''v.'' and ''n.'']   With a bounce; suddenly.
{{smaller block|<poem>Rapp’d at the door, nor stay’d to ask,
But ''bounce'' into the parlour entered.</poem>
{{right|''Gray'', Long Story.}}}}

'''bounceable''' (boun′sạ-bl), ''a.''   [< ''bounce'' + ''-able''.]   '''1.''' Capable of being bounced, as a ball.—'''2.''' Inclined to bounce, or lie. [Rare.]

'''bouncer''' (boun′sėr), ''n.''   [< ''bounce'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' One who or that which bounces.—'''2.''' Something big or large of its kind. {{smaller block|The stone must be a ''bouncer.'' {{right|''De Quincey.''}}}}
'''3.''' A large, strong, vigorous person: as, she is a ''bouncer.''—'''4.''' A strong muscular fellow kept in a hotel, restaurant, or other public resort, to bounce or expel disorderly persons. [Slang, U. S.]—'''5.''' A liar; a boaster; a bully.—'''6.''' A barefaced lie. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|But you are not deceiving me? You know the first time you came into my shop what a ''bouncer'' you told me.
{{right|''Colman the Younger'', John Bull, ii. 3.}}}}

'''bouncing''' (boun′sing), ''p. a.''   [Ppr. of ''bounce'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' Vigorous; strong; stout: as, “the ''bouncing'' Amazon,” Shak., M. N. D., ii. 2; “a ''bouncing'' lass,” ''Bulwer'', Pelham, xlix.—'''2.''' Exaggerated; excessive; big. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|<poem>We have had a merry and a lusty ordinary,
And wine, and good meat, and a ''bouncing'' reckoning.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Wildgoose Chase, i. 2.}}}}
'''3.''' Lying; bragging; boastful.
{{smaller block|I never saw such a ''bouncing'', swaggering puppy since I was born. {{right|''Goldsmith'', She Stoops to Conquer, iii.}}}}

'''bouncing-bet''' (boun′sing-bet′), ''n.''   [That is, ''bouncing Bet; Bet, Betsy'', familiar forms of ''Elizabeth.'']   A name of the common soapwort, ''Saponaria officinalis.'' See ''Saponaria.''

'''bouncingly''' (boun′sing-li), ''adv.'' Boastingly.   ''Barrow'', Pope’s Supremacy.

'''bound'''<sup>1</sup> (bound), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''bownde, bowne;'' < ME. ''bounde, boune, bunne,'' < OF. ''bunne, bonne, bone, bune,'' also ''bunde, bonde'' (AF. ''bounde''), earlier ''bodne,'' < ML. ''bodina, bodena'' (also, after OF., ''bunna, bonna''), earlier ''butina,'' a bound, limit. Cf. ''bourn''<sup>2</sup>, a variant of the same word.]   '''1.''' That which limits or circumscribes; an external or limiting line; hence, that which keeps in or restrains; limit; confine: as, the love of money knows no ''bounds''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Illimitable ocean, without ''bound'',
Without dimension! ''Milton'', P. L., ii. 892.</poem>
<poem>The dismal night—a night
In which the ''bounds'' of heaven and earth were lost.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Coming of Arthur.}}}}
{{smaller block|But the power of the West-Saxon ruler stretched beyond the ''bounds'' of Wessex, where, eastward of the Andredsweald, the so-called “Eastern Kingdom” grouped itself round the centre of Kent.
{{right|''J. R. Green'', Conq. of Eng., p. 65.}}}}
'''2.''' ''pl.'' The territory included within boundary-lines; domain.
{{smaller block|These rascals who come hither to annoy a noble lady on my ''bounds''. {{right|''Scott'', Peveril, I. vii.}}}}
'''3.''' A limited portion or piece of land, enjoyed by the owner of it in respect of tin only, and by virtue of an ancient prescription or liberty for encouragement to the tinners.   ''Pryce.'' [Cornwall.]—'''Butts and bounds.''' {{smaller|See ''butt''<sup>2</sup>.}}—'''To beat the bounds†''', {{smaller|to trace out the boundaries of a parish by touching certain points with a rod.}} ='''Syn. 1.''' {{smaller|''Border'', ''Confine'', etc. See ''boundary''.}}

'''bound'''<sup>1</sup> (bound), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''bounden'', < ''bounde'', n.]   '''1†.''' To confine within fixed limits; restrain by limitation.
{{smaller block|O God! I could be ''bounded'' in a nut-shell, and count myself a king of infinite space, were it not that I have bad dreams. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>It is not Italy, nor France, nor Europe,
That must ''bound'' me, if my fates call me forth.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Volpone, ii. 1.}}}}

'''2.''' To serve as a limit to; constitute the extent of; restrain in amount, degree, etc.: as, to ''bound'' our wishes by our means.
{{smaller block|<poem>Quaff immortality and joy, secure
Of surfeit, where full measure only ''bounds''
Excess.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., v. 639.}}}}

'''3.''' To form or constitute the boundary of; serve as a bound or limit to: as, the Pacific ocean ''bounds'' the United States on the west.
{{smaller block|The lasting dominion of Rome was ''bounded'' by the Rhine and the Danube.
{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Amer. Lects., p. 107.}}}}

'''4.''' To name the boundaries of: as, to ''bound'' the State of New York. ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|To circumscribe, restrict, hem in, border.}}

'''bound'''<sup>2</sup> (bound), ''v.''   [First in early mod. E.; < F. ''bondir'', leap, bound, orig. make a loud resounding noise; perhaps < LL. ''bombitare'', hum, buzz, freq. verb < L. ''bombus'', a humming or buzzing, > ''bomb''<sup>2</sup>, q. v.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To leap; jump; spring; move by leaps.
{{smaller block|Before his lord the ready spaniel ''bounds''.
{{right|''Pope'', Windsor Forest, l. 99.}}}}

'''2.''' To rebound, as an elastic ball. ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|''Leap, Spring'', etc. See ''skip'', ''v. i.''}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To cause to leap. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|If I might buffet for my love, or ''bound'' my horse for her favours, I could lay on like a butcher, and sit like a jack-an-apes, never off.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., v. 2.}}}}

'''2.''' To cause to rebound: as, to ''bound'' a ball.

'''bound'''<sup>2</sup> (bound), ''n.''   [< ''bound''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' A leap onward or upward; a jump; a rebound.
{{smaller block|The horses started with a sudden ''bound''.
{{right|''Addison.''}}}}
{{smaller block|These inward disgusts are but the first ''bounds'' of this ball of contention. {{right|''Decay of Christ. Piety.''}}}}
'''2.''' In ''ordnance,'' the path of a shot between two grazes: generally applied to the horizontal distance passed over by the shot between the points of impact.

'''bound'''<sup>3</sup> (bound), ''p. a.''   [Pp. of ''bind;'' as an adj., in the sense of obligatory, usually in the fuller form, ''bounden,'' < ME. ''bounden,'' < AS. ''bunden,'' pp. of ''bindan,'' bind: see ''bind.'']   '''1.''' Made fast by a band, tie, or bond; specifically, in fetters or chains; in the condition of a prisoner.
{{smaller block|Now Annas had sent him ''bound'' unto Caiaphas.
{{right|John xviii. 24.}}}}
Hence—'''2.''' Made fast by other than physical bonds.
{{smaller block|We are ''bound'' together for good or for evil in our great political interests.
{{right|''D. Webster'', Speech, Pittsburgh, July, 1833.}}}}
'''3.''' Confined; restrained; restricted; held firmly.
{{smaller block|Besides all this, he was ''bound'' to certain tributes all more or less degrading. {{right|''Brougham.''}}}}
Hence—'''4.''' Obliged by moral, legal, or compellable ties; under obligation or compulsion.
{{smaller block|When the case had been heard, it was evident to all men that the bishop had done only what he was ''bound'' to do.
